newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FEATURE - European art's finest heads for U.S.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - European art's finest heads for U.S.

text.p: Europe's biggest fine arts fair marks its 10th anniversary this month with a record number of participating dealers and plans to form an offshoot across the Atlantic.

In the decade since its creation through the merger of two leading Dutch antiques and Old Masters fairs, TEFAF Maastricht has expanded steadily to become one of the biggest events on the international art calendar.
Up to 70,000 visitors are expected in the prosperous southern Dutch market town of Maastricht during the fair, which started on Saturday and runs until March 16.

The fair's explosive growth prompted its organisers to launch a Basle offshoot in 1995 focusing on antiquities, pre-Columbian and Oriental art, and now they are looking to set up a similar event in the United States.
"We are looking into the possibilities of organising a fine arts fair in the United States in 2000," TEFAF general secretary Leo Lemmens told a news conference this month.
Spokeswoman Cornelie Langhout says the new fair will be geared to the demands of the U.S. market.
"It won't be a clone of what we do here -- it will have its own identity, which in turn will depend on whether we decide to locate on the east or west coast," she says.
Right now, however, The European Fine Art Foundation, a non-profit organisation led by dealers, is gearing up for its biggest fair yet.
"There are 12 more dealers taking part this year, boosting the total to around 170," says Langhout.

Each dealer shows an average of 10 to 20 pieces, with specialities ranging from classical antiquities through Old Master paintings and prints to contemporary art and modern jewellery from the world's biggest houses.
Highlights among this year's offerings include "Two cows and a bull beside a fence, a view of a town beyond" painted in 1647 by Paulus Potter.
One of the three best-known works by this short-lived Rembrandt contemporary from Haarlem near Amsterdam, the painting is being offered for sale by New York-based Old Master specialist Otto Naumann.

Other Old Masters featured in the fair's traditionally strong paintings and drawings section are a winter scene with skaters and sleigh-riders by Salomon van Ruysdael and a landscape with shepherds by Albert Cuyp -- both offered by New York-based French & Company.

A lucky find closer to home is the portrait of a "Young Woman playing the Viola da Gamba" by Gerrit van Honthorst, thought to be a sister piece to the "Woman playing a Violin" in the collection of The Hague's prestigious Mauritshuis museum.
Amsterdam art dealer Peter de Boer said he and several other Dutch dealers had clubbed together to buy the painting at auction in London in 1993.

"We were surprised at the favourable price...until it transpired that an acknowledged expert on Van Honthorst, Professor J.R Judson, was planning to classify the piece as a studio copy in his forthcoming book," De Boer said.

A flurry of correspondence with Judson on the merits of their piece versus the supposed original was finally resolved when De Boer loaded the canvas in the back of his car and invited Judson for a rendezvous with the rival painting in Heylshof, a small private museum in Worms, Germany.

"When we got there it wasn't difficult to see which canvas was the real one," De Boer said. "Our painting was finally authenticated by Judson, who found the German canvas to be a good studio version."
The Fair's 20th Century Art section, initially regarded as one of its weaker elements, has gone from strength to strength.
This year it features a string of highly covetable works, including a Chagall never before offered for sale.
Painted in 1970, the cheery "Clown, violiniste et aines" was acquired direct from the artist's estate by Amsterdam dealer Kunsthandel Frans Jacobs.

Also on offer are a trio of works by Fernand Leger, including "La Grande Parade", which inspired the eponymous blockbuster exhibition mounted by Amsterdam's Stedelijk Museum in 1984 as a tribute to retiring museum director Edy de Wilde.

"La Grande Parade" is being shown by the New York-based Barbara Mathes Gallery, while Paris's Galerie Piltzer is offering the later "La Parade" and an early "Composition aux Cles", priced at $2 million each.
